exam_guide_revision: Reviewed v5, 2026-09-26. This is a practical Data Structures & Algorithms track built around developer problems, code, performance, state, transfer, and pattern recognition.

learning_design.unlock_rule: All learning reveals are required. Each node moves quickly through a concrete problem, the obvious failure/waste, the maintained state or invariant that fixes it, the pattern name, a different real-world transfer, and one quick check.
learning_design.mastery_note: The goal is not to enjoy studying algorithms. The goal is to recognize the structure fast enough that an unfamiliar problem starts to look like a problem you have already solved.

authoring_notes: Anti-boring rule set: no optional reveals; no definition-first nodes; no university-course voice; no fake corporate narrative; start with code/data/workload; expose the waste or bug; name the useful state; then name the pattern; finish with transfer.

nodes.title: Make each folder solve the same smaller problem

reveal.text: Compute the total bytes under a directory that can contain files and child directories. You are learning to define one recursive call as a contract over a smaller subtree.

spans.text: Compute the total bytes under a directory that can contain files and child directories.

reveal.text: Thinking 'recursion means call the function again' gives no reason the process will stop or what each call returns. Takeaway: recursive syntax exists without a shrinking subproblem or return contract.

spans.text: recursive syntax exists without a shrinking subproblem or return contract

reveal.text: Contract: `total_bytes(dir)` returns total bytes in that directory subtree. Each child directory is a smaller instance; an empty subtree contributes 0. Takeaway: a smaller subproblem with the same promised return value.

spans.text: a smaller subproblem with the same promised return value

reveal.text: Recursive subtree contract. Trigger: hierarchical data where each child has the same problem shape as the parent

reveal.text: Org charts, UI trees, JSON trees, file systems, and ASTs all let a child solve the same kind of subproblem. Takeaway: self-similar hierarchy + strictly smaller child subproblems.

spans.text: self-similar hierarchy + strictly smaller child subproblems

reveal.text: What must get smaller on each recursive call? Answer: The subtree / remaining hierarchical subproblem.

modules.title: Choose tree traversal from the output dependency

nodes.title: Traversal order is just 'when must the parent act relative to the children?'

reveal.text: Some resource trees must delete children before parent; inherited config must flow parent before descendants. You are learning to choose preorder/postorder/inorder from dependency timing instead of memorizing names.

spans.text: Some resource trees must delete children before parent; inherited config must flow parent before descendants.
You are learning to choose preorder/postorder/inorder from dependency timing instead of memorizing names

reveal.text: Picking DFS order by habit can violate the actual dependency: deleting parent first may make children inaccessible or invalid. Takeaway: the processing order contradicts parent/child dependency.

spans.text: the processing order contradicts parent/child dependency

reveal.text: Parent before children → preorder. Children before parent → postorder. In a BST, left-node-right inorder exposes key order. Takeaway: when node work must happen relative to child work.

reveal.text: Traversal-order selection. Trigger: hierarchical processing has explicit before/after dependencies

reveal.text: Apply permissions downward with preorder; aggregate or delete upward with postorder. Takeaway: dependency timing determines traversal order.

spans.text: dependency timing determines traversal order

reveal.text: Delete descendants before directory: preorder or postorder? Answer: Postorder.

spans.text: Postorder.

nodes.title: Need hierarchy depth? Process one layer before the next

reveal.text: An organization report must group people by management distance from the CEO. You are learning to use a FIFO frontier when the output is organized by tree depth.

spans.text: An organization report must group people by management distance from the CEO.
You are learning to use a FIFO frontier when the output is organized by tree depth

reveal.text: Depth-first traversal can dive through five management levels before visiting another direct report. Takeaway: DFS visit order does not match the required layer order.

spans.text: DFS visit order does not match the required layer order

reveal.text: Use a queue. Process all depth-d nodes before the depth-(d+1) children they enqueue. Takeaway: a FIFO frontier ordered by distance from the root.

spans.text: a FIFO frontier ordered by distance from the root

reveal.text: Tree BFS / level order. Trigger: group or process nodes by depth / number of edges from root

spans.text: Tree BFS / level order
group or process nodes by depth / number of edges from root

reveal.text: UI nesting levels, filesystem depth reports, and minimum-edge tree distances have the same layer frontier. Takeaway: FIFO discovery preserves nondecreasing depth.

spans.text: FIFO discovery preserves nondecreasing depth

reveal.text: Who appears before grandchildren in level order? Answer: All direct children of the root.

spans.text: All direct children of the root.

nodes.title: A BST comparison lets you ignore an entire subtree — if the tree is actually well-shaped

reveal.text: An in-memory ordered index stores unique keys in a binary search tree. You are learning to use the BST order invariant to choose one child and understand why complexity depends on height.

reveal.text: Searching both subtrees ignores the BST property; claiming O(log n) for every unbalanced BST ignores height. Takeaway: either order information is wasted or performance is overstated.

spans.text: either order information is wasted or performance is overstated

reveal.text: Compare target with current key and follow only the side that can contain it. Complexity is O(h); balancing is what keeps h near log n. Takeaway: current node + ordering invariant over its subtrees.

binary tree with a maintained key-order invariant

reveal.text: Ordered maps/sets may use balanced trees to support lookup plus predecessor/successor operations. Takeaway: comparison discards one ordered subtree.

reveal.text: Target 32 at node 50: which side remains possible? Answer: The left subtree.

modules.title: Index prefixes instead of rescanning strings

nodes.title: Autocomplete is easier when shared prefixes literally share a path

reveal.text: A CLI stores commands like `deploy`, `describe`, and `delete` and frequently asks for suggestions after `de`. You are learning to recognize a trie when queries are about shared string prefixes rather than only exact equality.

spans.text: A CLI stores commands like `deploy`, `describe`, and `delete` and frequently asks for suggestions after `de`.
You are learning to recognize a trie when queries are about shared string prefixes rather than only exact equality

reveal.text: A hash set is excellent for exact membership but does not directly expose all keys beginning with a prefix. Takeaway: exact-key indexing does not organize keys by shared beginnings.

spans.text: exact-key indexing does not organize keys by shared beginnings

reveal.text: Consume characters along a path. Keys with the same prefix reuse the same early nodes; reaching `de` gives a focused subtree of candidates. Takeaway: the trie node reached after consuming the query prefix.

spans.text: the trie node reached after consuming the query prefix

reveal.text: Trie / prefix tree. Trigger: autocomplete, keys-with-prefix, or longest-prefix style queries

spans.text: Trie / prefix tree
autocomplete, keys-with-prefix, or longest-prefix style queries

reveal.text: Command completion, dictionary suggestions, and prefix routing all reuse shared prefix paths. Takeaway: shared prefixes become shared path state.

spans.text: shared prefixes become shared path state

reveal.text: After walking prefix `de`, where should suggestion search begin? Answer: At the trie node reached by `de`, not back at the root.

spans.text: At the trie node reached by `de`, not back at the root.

glossary.definition: A tree-like index whose path edges/steps represent successive characters or symbols of keys.
The beginning portion of a string key.

nodes.title: A path can exist without the shorter key being stored

reveal.text: The trie contains `deploy-prod`. Does that automatically mean exact key `deploy` exists? You are learning to separate prefix-path existence from full-key existence with terminal state.

spans.text: The trie contains `deploy-prod`. Does that automatically mean exact key `deploy` exists?
You are learning to separate prefix-path existence from full-key existence with terminal state

reveal.text: Returning true after successfully walking every character of `deploy` would incorrectly treat every prefix of a longer command as a registered command. Takeaway: path existence is confused with complete-key membership.

spans.text: path existence is confused with complete-key membership

reveal.text: Mark nodes where a complete key ends. Exact lookup requires both a valid path and a terminal/value marker at the final node. Takeaway: terminal/value state at the final prefix node.

spans.text: terminal/value state at the final prefix node

reveal.text: Trie terminal marker. Trigger: some stored keys are prefixes of other keys

spans.text: Trie terminal marker
some stored keys are prefixes of other keys

reveal.text: Route registries, command registries, and dictionaries all need to distinguish 'prefix exists' from 'full key exists'. Takeaway: complete-key state is separate from path state.

spans.text: complete-key state is separate from path state

reveal.text: Trie has only `apple`. Is `app` automatically an exact stored key? Answer: No — only if the `app` node is terminal.

spans.text: No — only if the `app` node is terminal.

nodes.title: Once you reach the prefix node, ignore the rest of the trie

reveal.text: A routing-style table needs the longest stored prefix matching the beginning of a query key. You are learning to turn the reached prefix/path node into the frontier for focused descendant or longest-prefix work.

spans.text: A routing-style table needs the longest stored prefix matching the beginning of a query key.
You are learning to turn the reached prefix/path node into the frontier for focused descendant or longest-prefix work

reveal.text: Scanning every stored key compares unrelated prefixes again and again. Takeaway: global search ignores the prefix structure already traversed.

spans.text: global search ignores the prefix structure already traversed

reveal.text: Walk the query path once. For autocomplete, enumerate descendants from the prefix node. For longest-prefix matching, remember the deepest terminal node encountered. Takeaway: the current prefix node plus terminal checkpoints on the path.

spans.text: the current prefix node plus terminal checkpoints on the path

reveal.text: Trie prefix query. Trigger: query result depends on all keys under a prefix or the deepest matching prefix

spans.text: Trie prefix query

reveal.text: Autocomplete and longest-prefix routing differ in output but reuse the same prefix-path traversal. Takeaway: the prefix path narrows the search frontier.

spans.text: the prefix path narrows the search frontier

reveal.text: For longest stored prefix, what should you remember while walking the query? Answer: The deepest terminal/value-bearing node seen so far.
